papers.title: A Comprehensive AI-Powered Survey Platform for Streamlining Data Collection,Analytical Power for Smart E-Governance
papers.abstract: Socio-economic data collection for national policy is undergoing a paradigm shift with the emergence of AI-driven automation and analytical frameworks.Existing statistical systems, such as those managed by the Ministry of Statistics and Programme Implementation (MoSPI) through the National Sample Survey (NSS), often rely on fragmented, manual, and enumerator-driven processes that lack real-time validation and linguistic inclusivity. This survey explores the state of the art in no-code survey generation, qualitative guidelines for software research , and smart e-governance through open data and big data analytics. By analyzing recent developments in data visualization tools and the "Statistics-as-a-Service" (StaaS) framework, this paper presents a unified AI-powered architecture that integrates multi-modal delivery with real-time monitoring and automated response validation.The proposed framework leverages advanced machine learning techniques to process large datasets, identifying patterns that improve decision-making in sectors like health, education, and agriculture.This architecture offers a scalable, trusted, and intelligent approach to modernizing national statistical challenges while supporting the vision of a citizen-centric digital governance ecosystem.

papers.title: Measuring Teaching Efficacy Through Comprehension Delta: Large Language Models as Standardized Learner Proxies
papers.abstract: Measuring teaching quality remains one of the most persistent challenges in educational research. Existing approaches depend on classroom observation protocols that require trained human raters, or on student evaluations that correlate poorly with actual learning outcomes. Both suffer from subjectivity, scalability constraints, and well-documented biases. This paper proposes a novel measurement construct, the dual-run comprehension delta, which reframes teaching efficacy as the measurable change in a standardized evaluator's comprehension before and after receiving a teacher's explanation. We argue that large language models can serve as controlled learner proxies for this purpose, and we develop a formal framework in which a domain-specific assessment is administered to an LLM twice: once without access to the teacher's explanation, and once with it. The score difference constitutes the delta. We ground this construct in established validity theory from the Standards for Educational and Psychological Testing, analyze it through the lens of pedagogical content knowledge and explanation quality research, and present a reference architecture that instantiates the methodology. We argue that the dual-run delta offers a reproducible and scalable complement to existing teaching quality measures, particularly suited for asynchronous instruction, teacher certification, and professional development contexts. We outline a validity argument organized around Kane's interpretation/use framework, discuss the construct boundaries of the approach, and identify the empirical studies required to evaluate its claims.

papers.title: Authorization-First Retrieval: Enforcing Least Privilege in Multi-Agent RAG Systems
papers.abstract: Enterprise deployments of Retrieval-Augmented Generation and multi-agent LLM systems routinely handle data subject to role-based access control, yet the semantic retrieval step in these pipelines bypasses conventional authorization enforcement. We formalize this gap as a pipeline ordering problem: once unauthorized content enters any model context, no downstream filter can provably undo its influence on generation. We introduce Authorization-First Retrieval (AFR), an architectural invariant requiring that authorization constrain the retrieval candidate set before any learned component consumes retrieved content. We prove AFR is a necessary condition for authorization correctness under the contextexposure model used by all major deployed RAG systems. We construct a controlled evaluation corpus of 43 chunks across 28 documents with role-scoped access rules spanning five enterprise roles, three sensitivity levels, and four domains. Against 93 structured queries covering six attack categories, retrieve-then-filter pipelines expose unauthorized context in 96.8% of queries and violate authorization correctness on 100% of queries that should be denied. AFR eliminates all structural leaks (0/93) and all answer leaks (0/93). A chunk-size sweep across five granularities confirms AFR holds invariant to chunking strategy, while retrieve-then-filter leakage increases monotonically with chunk size. Stress testing at retrieval depth exceeding corpus size shows AFR holds under worstcase saturation. We identify parametric knowledge leakage as a fundamental boundary on what retrieval architecture can guarantee.

papers.title: Toward a Philosophical Taxonomy of Bias in Large Language Models: A Survey
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have become central to many applications, but their rapid adoption raises serious concerns about fairness and bias. This survey introduces a philosophical taxonomy that reframes LLM bias, organizing existing work around three core areas: bias evaluation, bias mitigation, and evaluation of mitigation techniques. We distinguish between substantial harms (tangible, adverse impacts on individuals or groups) and representational harms (demeaning or stereotyping portrayals that violate dignity), and highlight how these harms often interact and reinforce one another. By structuring metrics, datasets, and methods within this taxonomy, the survey provides a foundation for developing fairer and more inclusive language models (LMs).
